title: Blockchain Basics: Trust Without a Middleman

questions.question: The primary problem a blockchain solves is:
options: Letting parties who do not trust each other share one tamper-evident ledger without a central keeper
Making databases run faster than SQL
Encrypting files so only the owner can read them
Compressing transactions to save storage
questions.rationale: A bank normally arbitrates disputes; a blockchain replaces that arbiter with replicated copies plus consensus rules, making unilateral rewriting of history economically infeasible. It is slower than a normal database - its value is trustlessness, not speed.

questions.question: A good cryptographic hash function has the property that:
options: A one-bit change in input scrambles the output completely
The input can be recovered from the hash
Two different inputs often share a hash
Output length depends on input length
questions.rationale: The avalanche effect means the tiniest edit produces a wholly different digest, which is what makes hashes usable as tamper-seals. Hashes are one-way (irreversible), collision-resistant, and fixed-length regardless of input.

questions.question: Each block in a blockchain contains, among other things:
options: The hash of the previous block
The private keys of all users
The bank's approval signature
A backup of all earlier blocks
questions.rationale: Storing the previous block's hash welds blocks together: altering any old block changes its hash, visibly breaking every later block. Blocks also carry a Merkle root, timestamp and nonce - but never private keys.

questions.question: Tampering with a transaction in block 100 requires the attacker to:
options: Re-mine block 100 and every block after it faster than the honest network
Only rewrite block 100
Obtain the network administrator's password
Delete the recipient's copy of the chain
questions.rationale: Changing block 100 changes its hash, so block 101's stored reference breaks; the attacker must redo the work for all subsequent blocks AND outpace honest miners extending the real chain. Immutability is economic, not magical.

questions.question: In Bitcoin's proof of work, the right to append the next block is earned by:
options: Being first to solve a computational hash puzzle
Holding the most bitcoins
Being elected by validators
Paying the highest fee
questions.rationale: Miners race to find a nonce making the block hash fall below a target; solving first earns block rewards plus fees. Proof of stake instead selects validators by capital staked - Ethereum's mechanism since 2022.

questions.question: A transaction is signed with the sender's:
options: Private key, and verified by anyone using the public key
Public key, and verified with the private key
Password and a CAPTCHA
Bank's master key
questions.rationale: Digital signatures: sign with the secret, verify with the public. Ownership in blockchain reduces to private-key possession - lose the key and the funds are unreachable forever, since there is no bank to appeal to.

questions.question: A smart contract is best described as:
options: A program on the blockchain that executes automatically when its conditions are met
A legal document scanned onto the blockchain
A handshake agreement between two miners
An insurance policy against hacks
questions.rationale: Smart contracts are self-executing code - a vending machine for agreements. Their rigidity is the feature (no intermediary can interfere) and the bug (a flawed contract is expensive or impossible to patch, as billion-dollar exploits have shown).

questions.question: A consortium of banks wants a shared ledger among known, regulated participants. The most sensible choice is:
options: A permissioned (private) blockchain such as Hyperledger
The public Bitcoin network
No blockchain at all is impossible
A social media platform
questions.rationale: When participants are known and regulation matters more than censorship-resistance, permissioned chains give control, privacy and throughput that open networks cannot. Public chains suit open, trustless environments.

questions.question: A 51% attack refers to:
options: One party controlling the majority of the network's mining power or stake
Stealing 51% of the coins
A bug that corrupts 51% of blocks
Losing 51% of your private key
questions.rationale: Majority control lets an attacker censor transactions or reorganise recent blocks - the reason small networks with little total hash power are far easier to attack than Bitcoin's planet-scale footprint.

questions.question: The scaling debate in blockchain is driven by:
options: Base layers processing far fewer transactions per second than card networks
Blocks being too large to download
Electricity being too cheap
Too many banks adopting the technology
questions.rationale: Bitcoin handles around 7 transactions per second versus tens of thousands for card networks. Solutions split into layer-1 redesigns (bigger/faster base chains) and layer-2 systems like payment channels and rollups that batch off-chain and settle on-chain.
